items.stem: A document-classification pipeline processes 400,000 records weekly. The quality team reviews every customer complaint and every classifier-flagged output, but never samples outputs scored high-confidence. Which addition closes the monitoring gap?

opts.t: Add per-segment breakdowns to the existing weekly dashboard.
Raise the confidence classifier's threshold so fewer records qualify as high-confidence.
Add stratified sampling of the high-confidence stream, across segments and verdict classes.
Rely on the existing complaint and flagged-output reviews, since together they already cover the error types that occur.

items.whyRight: The unsampled high-confidence stream is exactly where a novel error pattern first appears, since it never reaches a human through a complaint or a flag. Stratified sampling across segments and verdict classes gives the quality team visibility into that stream instead of waiting for a complaint.

whyWrong.A: Per-segment dashboard breakdowns fix aggregate masking on data already collected; they add nothing for records that were never sampled in the first place.
whyWrong.B: Narrowing the high-confidence label shrinks the unreviewed population without validating any of the records still inside it, leaving the same blind spot smaller but unmeasured.
whyWrong.D: The stem's own gap is that high-confidence records are never sampled, so complaints and flags cannot already cover error types that surface only in that unreviewed stream.

items.t1Clause: The stem states the pipeline 'never samples' the high-confidence stream; invert to 'already stratifies sampling across the high-confidence stream but the weekly dashboard reports only an aggregate average,' and per-segment breakdowns becomes the fix.
items.factAnswerRaw: Add stratified sampling of the high-confidence stream

items.stem: A multi-tenant billing assistant must never state another customer's account identifier in a reply, and the compliance officer requires this metric defined before sign-off. Which threshold should the team set?

opts.t: A deterministic pattern or field scan enforced as a hard zero — 0 occurrences per N replies.
Re-anchor the bar to a small non-zero rate, such as fewer than 0.1% of 10,000 replies.
Calibrate the pass bar once a full month of baseline reply volume has been observed.
Log every reply and flag any that mention another customer's account number for review afterward.

items.whyRight: The requirement is exact and machine-checkable — a specific customer's account identifier either appears in the text or it does not. Code can enforce that boundary precisely, so the metric is a deterministic hard zero measured per N replies, not a rate description chosen after results arrive.

whyWrong.B: This re-anchoring move belongs to an open-ended, model-judged property; this requirement is exact and code-checkable, so a non-zero statistical rate weakens an enforceable boundary into a tolerance.
whyWrong.C: Waiting for baseline volume turns the bar into a description of whatever the system already does, and a deterministic property needs no baseline to define its threshold.
whyWrong.D: Flagging after emission only detects a violation that has already reached the customer; the requirement calls for a hard zero enforced before the reply ships, not a review queue afterward.

items.t1Clause: The requirement is deterministically checkable ('must never state another customer's account identifier'); invert to an open-ended, model-judged property (e.g., reply tone) proposed at a 0% bar, and re-anchoring to a small non-zero rate becomes the fix.

items.stem: A coding assistant generates candidate functions behind a test harness that automatically reruns generation up to five times until the tests pass, before any code reaches a reviewer. Which aggregation should the engineering lead adopt to report reliability?

opts.t: `pass@k` — credit the harness for reachable success across the up-to-five attempts.
`pass^k` = 1.0 applied to every attempt, since each rerun is treated as customer-visible.
`pass^k`, since five attempts is a large enough sample to detect hidden instability.
Skip aggregation and rely on the reviewer, since every generated candidate already reaches human review.

items.whyRight: The test harness catches and reruns failing attempts before any output is exposed, so what matters is whether a passing candidate is reachable within the attempt budget. `pass@k` measures exactly that; the harness's own retries make individual-attempt reliability irrelevant to what the reviewer eventually sees.

whyWrong.B: Demanding a perfect first attempt across five retries ignores that the harness absorbs failures; this bar belongs to steps where a single silent failure reaches the world.
whyWrong.C: Attempt count measures how many times something was tried, not whether a failure is absorbed or exposed; that distinction, not the number five, decides the aggregation.
whyWrong.D: The stem places the harness before the reviewer stage, so only candidates that already passed the tests are ever seen; the reviewer never observes the failed attempts this option assumes.

items.t1Clause: The harness 'automatically reruns... before any code reaches a reviewer'; invert so every generated candidate deploys directly without passing through the harness, and pass^k becomes the correct aggregation.

items.stem: A contract-review assistant fabricates clause numbers only for contracts uploaded in the past week; older contracts are still handled correctly. The legal-ops lead wants this fixed before next week's compliance audit. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Move to a higher-capability model, since fabricated clause numbers signal a reasoning limitation.
Add an explicit system-prompt instruction not to state clause numbers it cannot verify.
Expand the evaluation set with more contract examples to measure the fabrication rate precisely.
Check how the newly uploaded contracts were chunked and indexed, since the failure is confined to that recent batch.

items.whyRight: The failure is confined to one recent batch of documents while everything else still works, which is the data-coverage and chunking signature, not a model deficiency. Checking how the new contracts were chunked and indexed tests the layer the symptom actually points to, before any model change is considered.

whyWrong.A: Fabrication confined to one recent batch is a data-layer signature, not a reasoning limitation; swapping models replaces a component the symptom never implicates.
whyWrong.B: An instruction not to overstate certainty treats the symptom, not the cause, and cannot conjure a clause number that was never correctly indexed in the first place.
whyWrong.C: A larger evaluation set would measure the fabrication rate more precisely without diagnosing which layer produces it, leaving the actual defect unaddressed before next week's audit.

items.t1Clause: The fabrication is 'confined to contracts uploaded in the past week'; invert to failure occurring broadly and uniformly with retrieval and chunking already verified clean, and moving to a higher-capability model becomes the fix.

items.stem: An agent pipeline has a p95 latency budget of 3 seconds and is currently averaging 4.1 seconds; no stage-level timing has been collected. Which action should the team take before changing anything?

opts.t: Enable prompt caching on the static portions of every request immediately.
Profile stage-level timing first to identify which stage dominates the overage.
Route routine requests to a smaller cascade model to cut generation time.
Reduce the retrieved passages sent to the model, since retrieval is clearly the slowest stage.

items.whyRight: Halving a stage that accounts for only a fraction of the total budget barely moves the aggregate number, so the first move is to measure which stage actually owns the 1.1-second overage. Every optimization lever below is real, but none of them is targeted until that measurement exists.

whyWrong.A: Caching is a real lever with no quality cost, but committing to it before profiling assumes the static preamble is the dominant stage, which the stem never establishes.
whyWrong.C: Cascade routing is a genuine lever elsewhere, but its trigger must be validated per segment; applying it before profiling assumes generation is the dominant stage without evidence.
whyWrong.D: The stem states no stage-level timing exists yet, which directly contradicts the claim that retrieval is clearly the slowest stage.

items.t1Clause: The stem states 'no stage-level timing has been collected'; invert to timing already showing the static preamble dominates the budget, and enabling prompt caching becomes the fix.

notes: g41 (F-4.11-07, S1 normal): the ARCHETYPE-LEDGER's normal-direction gloss for S1 is 'the principle demands removing something; the distractors compensate instead,' which doesn't literally fit a measurement-first answer ('profile first' removes nothing). Kept S1 rather than substituting to S6 because the underlying mechanics still fit S1's stated column definition ('states a governing principle by name... apply it against options defensible on some other axis') — the governing principle is 'profile before optimizing,' and all three distractors are real 4.11 levers (caching, cascade routing, retrieval trimming) that are correct elsewhere but premature here. Flagging for the grounding audit to confirm this reading is acceptable rather than a forced fit.
